docs.title: gpex
docs.text:
Gaussian processes for experimental design in JAX.

gpex is a JAX library for Gaussian-process inference from values, derivatives, and other linear measurements. Combine different measurement types in one model, then predict the quantities you care about from the same posterior.

It is built for experimental design and Bayesian optimization involving a scalar latent function. gpex provides the posterior operations; you choose the acquisition strategy and experiment loop.

Get started Tutorials API reference

Alpha status

The mathematical model and core inference paths are implemented and tested. The package is still pre-1.0, so public names may change before the first stable release.

docs.title: Adding observations to an existing posterior
docs.text:
In JAX, growing a Cholesky factor changes array shapes and can trigger recompilation, even when the update itself is efficient. gpex combines Cholesky updates with reserved capacity so fixed-size observation batches can reuse compiled code.

Start with 512 observations, then add 512 more and predict after every update. gpex completes this workflow 38× faster than GPJax and 15× faster than GPyTorch on CPU, and 108× and 6.6× faster on the H100.

Float64, fixed hyperparameters, one prediction point per update. Times include initial conditioning and compilation, with numerical libraries initialized before timing. Bars show medians of three processes, with min–max ranges. Full benchmark and setup.

docs.title: Fit a model with values and predict the gradient
docs.text:
Condition on three function values, then predict gradients between those measurements. ObservationBlock.from_arrays creates the observation block directly from location and value arrays:

import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

import gpex as gpx
from gpex.operators import Identity, Gradient

x_obs = jnp.array([[-1.0], [0.0], [1.0]])
y = jnp.array([-0.8, 0.0, 0.8])
observations = gpx.FunctionalDataset([
    gpx.ObservationBlock.from_arrays(x_obs, y, operator=Identity(), variance=0.01, name="values")
])
gp = gpx.GaussianProcess(gpx.kernels.RBFKernel(lengthscale=0.7))
posterior = gp.condition(observations)

x_query = jnp.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, 51)[:, None]
query = gpx.FunctionalQuery([
    gpx.FunctionalBlock(x_query, operator=Gradient(), name="gradient"),
])
gradient_mean = posterior.predict_mean(query)["gradient"]  # shape (51, 1)

variance is the observation noise variance. The getting-started guide explains the array shapes and returned predictions step by step. For the mathematics behind combining measurement types, see Gaussian processes with linear functionals and the available operators.

Kernel and noise parameters can also be learned with maximum likelihood (MLE) or maximum a posteriori (MAP) fitting.

docs.title: Related libraries
docs.text:
The choice depends on the model and workflow you need:

Library Framework A useful choice when you need… gpex JAX Mixed linear measurements, differentiable design, and sequential inference that reuses compiled code and posterior factors within a fixed capacity. GPJax JAX A range of GP models and likelihoods, including classification and sparse variational inference. GPyTorch PyTorch Scalable exact and variational GP inference, multitask models, or neural-network integration. BoTorch PyTorch A Bayesian-optimization toolkit with built-in acquisition functions and acquisition optimizers.

gpex and GPJax both benefit from JAX's compiled execution. For small sequential experiments, however, compiling for each new dataset size can dominate the work. gpex's reserved observation blocks let the same compiled conditioning and update functions serve successive experiment steps. Choose capacity for the planned experiment, since reserved slots also cost memory and computation.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
These benchmarks measure conditioning, posterior updates, fitting and prediction on an Apple M3 Max CPU and an NVIDIA H100 GPU. We first measure individual operations, then follow changing datasets and sequential observations to include the cost of compilation over a complete workflow.

There are two useful timings:

  • Cold start: tracing, compilation and the first execution of a workload in an initialized runtime.
  • Warm runtime: execution after compilation. New data can use the same compiled function when array shapes, dtypes and static configuration stay the same.

Before timing, a tiny unrelated problem initializes the numerical libraries. That initialization, Python startup and input construction are excluded. Target compilation is fully timed, with persistent compilation caching disabled. CPU and GPU results appear side by side. Colors identify methods, solid lines show float32 and dashed lines show float64. Light bands show the range across three independent processes. Quoted examples use the recommended float64 precision. Curves stop at sizes chosen to keep runtime and memory use practical.

docs.title: Conditioning and prediction
docs.text:
Start with N function-value observations and predict the mean and covariance at one point. This measures covariance construction, dense factorization and prediction together.

result = gp.condition(dataset).predict(query)

At N = 32,768 on the H100, warm runtime is 345 ms for gpex, 320 ms for GPJax and 817 ms for GPyTorch. Peak device allocation is about 16, 16 and 48 GiB.

docs.title: Adding an observation
docs.text:
Once a posterior is available, adding an observation need not repeat the full factorization. Append updates the existing Cholesky factor. Rebuild conditions from scratch on the complete dataset. Both paths then predict at one point. The initial posterior is prepared outside timing.

result = posterior.append(Locations(points), values, block="values").predict(query)
result = gp.condition(complete).predict(query)  # rebuild

The warm-runtime row shows the cheaper factor update, while the cold-start row shows how much compilation adds to the first call. Each point uses storage for N+1 observations and measures one addition. To see what happens over many additions, we also need to account for compilation reuse.

docs.title: Conditioning on changing datasets
docs.text:
With compact datasets, growing the arrays changes their shapes and can trigger another JAX compilation. gpex's fixed-capacity observation blocks reserve storage and track the number of active observations. Unused slots do not affect the posterior. Keeping the same block structure, capacities, dtypes and query shapes lets successive datasets reuse the compiled conditioning function.

This benchmark isolates that benefit: every call builds a new posterior from scratch. Extra capacity costs memory and computation because the factorization covers the reserved system. It can still save time when it avoids compilation for each new dataset size.

condition_and_predict = eqx.filter_jit(
    lambda gp, dataset, query: gp.condition(dataset).predict(query)
)
for dataset in datasets:
    result = condition_and_predict(gp, dataset, query)
    jax.block_until_ready(result)

Each curve processes 100 independent datasets with 16–512 observations and predicts one value after each conditioning call. Every dataset size is distinct. Reserved gpex datasets keep capacity 512. “gpex · exact-size arrays” sets capacity to the actual number of observations. GPJax and GPyTorch also use arrays of that length. Cumulative time includes compilation and excludes input construction and validation.

docs.title: Sequential observations
docs.text:
Now keep the observations collected so far and add one at a time. Fixed capacity reuses compilation, while posterior append also reuses the factor. Comparing append with reconditioning shows the additional benefit of the factor update once compilation can be reused by both methods.

@eqx.filter_jit
def append_and_predict(posterior, points, values, query):
    posterior = posterior.append(Locations(points), values, block="values0")
    return posterior, posterior.predict(query)

Starting from 512 observations, add one observation and predict one value at each step until there are 1,024 observations. Both gpex methods reserve capacity 1,024. Append updates the factor, while rebuild conditions again on the updated dataset. GPJax reconditions on growing arrays. GPyTorch uses its incremental fantasy-update API. Totals include initial conditioning, every prediction and compilation.

In float64, the complete gpex append workflow takes 1.05 s on CPU and 0.83 s on the H100. Reconditioning takes 2.53 s and 0.79 s respectively. At these sizes, GPU append and reconditioning have similar total cost.

docs.title: MLE and MAP fitting
docs.text:
Fitting changes the kernel parameters, so each objective evaluation must account for a different covariance matrix. Here we optimize variance and lengthscale for 100 Adam steps with fixed observation noise. MAP also includes Gamma priors.

fitted = fit((gp, dataset), objective, optax.adam(0.02), step_count=100)

objective evaluates negative_log_marginal_likelihood(*model) for MLE or negative_log_posterior(*model) for MAP. Both timing rows show complete 100-step fit time divided by 100. Cold time includes compilation, amortized across those 100 steps. Warm time excludes it. At N = 16,384 in float64 on the H100, warm MLE and MAP each take 447 ms per average step.

docs.title: Differentiable design
docs.text:
Experimental design compares proposed measurements before their outcomes are known. We evaluate the remaining gradient variance at the origin after four proposed value measurements, then differentiate it with respect to their eight coordinates. Ordinary design appends the proposal to the conditioning state. Prepared design caches the fixed target query and evaluates its variance reduction directly. Initial conditioning and query preparation are outside timing.

jax.value_and_grad(design)(points, conditioning, query)
jax.value_and_grad(design_prepared)(points, prepared, variance)

At N = 32,768 on the H100, warm objective-and-gradient evaluation takes 52.6 ms for ordinary design and 20.2 ms for prepared design.

docs.title: Mixed measurements
docs.text:
The same conditioning operation can combine values, derivatives and averages. Here the dataset contains approximately equal numbers of function values, first derivatives and box averages with half-width 0.15. N counts scalar measurements across all three types.

result = gp.condition(dataset).predict(query)

Each call conditions on the complete dataset and predicts one value. Warm runtime is 366 ms for N = 32,768 on the H100 and 1.65 s for N = 8,192 on the CPU.

docs.title: Prediction batches
docs.text:
Keep the posterior fixed and vary the number of query points. Full prediction returns the joint query covariance. Marginal prediction returns individual variances without constructing that full matrix. Conditioning on 4,096 observations happens before timing.

result = posterior.predict(query)            # mean and full covariance
result = posterior.predict_marginals(query)  # mean and marginal variances

On the H100, one query takes 0.45 ms for full covariance and 0.44 ms for marginal variances. At 1,024 queries, warm runtime is 2.15 ms and 1.93 ms respectively. Peak memory includes the posterior.

docs.title: Hardware and timing
docs.text:
Setting Configuration CPU Apple M3 Max, 14 cores, 36 GiB unified memory GPU NVIDIA H100, approximately 93 GiB device memory, 32 allocated host cores Python 3.12.11 on CPU, 3.12.13 on GPU Software JAX/jaxlib 0.11.2, cholops 0.2.1, GPJax 1.0.0, PyTorch 2.14.0, GPyTorch 1.15.2 Model Zero-mean RBF GP, variance 1, lengthscale 0.8, noise variance 0.05 Arithmetic Separate float32 and float64 runs, highest matrix-multiplication precision

Regression uses evenly spaced inputs on [-4, 4] and values from sin(1.7*x) + 0.1*cos(3.1*x). Kernels, input dimensions, observation geometry, noise and prediction batch size can all change the cost.

Each process first runs Cholesky factorization, triangular solves and matrix multiplication on an unrelated seven-row problem. This loads numerical libraries without compiling the measured workload. Initialization is recorded separately and excluded from all timing curves. Cold start therefore represents an existing application encountering a new workload or array shape, not launching Python.

The single-operation plots show cold and warm timing separately where indicated. Append and rebuild also show both timings. Design and prediction plots show warm execution from prepared state.

Each ordinary point is the median of three independent process medians. Each process measures 20 synchronized warm calls, five complete fits, or two updates, depending on the workload. Cold timing uses one first call per process. Light bands show the process min–max range, not a confidence interval. Complete workflows have three process samples and include compilation in their cumulative timings. GPyTorch runs eagerly, so its cold time is the first execution without a separate compilation phase.

CPU runs use library-default threading. The benchmark harness synchronizes JAX results and runs numerical checks outside timing. Single-operation conditioning uses exact capacity. Append reserves one additional observation, and ordinary design reserves the four proposed observations.

Memory is the largest recorded peak across the three processes. CPU memory is peak process RSS, including setup and compilation. GPU memory is peak live device allocation, excluding host memory and unused pool capacity. Both use the same scale across precisions within a figure. The initialization pass can contribute to the recorded peak.

Training jitter is 1e-6 in gpex and GPJax. GPJax also uses predictive jitter of 1e-6.

GPU runs use CUDA 13 with NVIDIA driver 595.91.07 or 615.71.09, depending on the allocated node. The host CPU is an AMD EPYC 9554. Driver and node differences can affect compilation and runtime. Within each precision, related workloads and their comparison libraries run serially on the same allocated GPU. Different groups can use different nodes, so small differences across groups should not be interpreted as controlled comparisons on identical systems. Each job stages the compiler, runtime and source on node-local storage before measurement. Staging is excluded from the curves. Every worker disables xla_gpu_experimental_enable_fusion_autotuner to avoid expensive fusion candidate compilation. GPJax is pinned to commit 964bad77483e3c694f116d666d21617a1260208b.

docs.title: Reproduce the measurements
docs.text:
Install the locked comparison dependencies and profile a smaller grid locally:

uv sync --locked --all-groups
XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_experimental_enable_fusion_autotuner=false \
JAX_DEFAULT_MATMUL_PRECISION=highest \
uv run --frozen --group comparison python benchmarks/run.py \
  --workloads dense gpjax gpytorch --sizes 256 1024 4096 \
  --dtype float64 --process-samples 3 --repeats 20 \
  --output results/local.json
uv run --frozen python benchmarks/plot.py --results results/local.json \
  --output-dir results/figures

Repeat with --dtype float32 and a separate output path for single precision. The benchmark runner documentation describes workloads, settings, numerical checks and report fields.

These figures measure library source 5ffd0bff6d9ec8ba75f181ecccb7ecdb67568a2a. The profiling branch contains the campaign plan, plot generator and compact measurements in profiling/results/4e5cada.json. CPU measurements use profiling revision 683bade, and GPU measurements use 4e5cada. Their library source, locked dependencies, scientific workloads and timing protocol match.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
gpex requires Python 3.12 or newer and JAX 0.11.2.

Install the released package from PyPI:

pip install gpex

Or install the latest development version from GitHub:

pip install "git+https://github.com/avrohr/gpex.git@main"

To run the tutorials locally, install uv, then clone the repository and install the optional notebook dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/avrohr/gpex.git
cd gpex
uv sync --extra examples
uv run jupyter lab docs/tutorials/first-posterior.ipynb

JAX selects the CPU backend by default. Follow the JAX installation guide when you need a platform-specific accelerator build.

docs.title: Floating precision
docs.text:
Float64 is recommended for numerical robustness. Enable it before importing gpex or constructing arrays:

import jax

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

Use JAX's default floating dtype throughout model parameters, locations, readings, and queries. Mixed dtypes are unsupported. Float32 is supported when x64 is disabled, with less accuracy available for nearly noiseless measurements, small posterior variances, and tightly converged fits.

docs.title: Build a dataset
docs.text:
A FunctionalBlock describes what to measure: locations, a linear operator, and a name. Here, Identity means function values. An ObservationDesignBlock adds the measurement noise variance, and an ObservationBlock attaches the observed readings. A FunctionalDataset collects one or more observation blocks.

Locations use shape (n, d): n rows of measurement locations, each containing d input coordinates. Here there are three locations in one dimension, so the shape is (3, 1). Coordinates must have a floating-point dtype.

import jax.numpy as jnp

from gpex import (
    FunctionalBlock,
    FunctionalDataset,
    ObservationBlock,
    ObservationDesignBlock,
    operators,
)

points = jnp.array([[-1.0], [0.0], [1.0]])
readings = jnp.array([-0.8, 0.0, 0.8])

functional = FunctionalBlock(
    locations=points,
    operator=operators.Identity(),
    name="observed_values",
)
design = ObservationDesignBlock(
    functional=functional, variance=0.01, max_size=points.shape[0],
)
observations = ObservationBlock(design=design, y=readings)
dataset = FunctionalDataset(blocks=[observations])

For convenience, ObservationBlock.from_arrays constructs the functional and design blocks for you. It defaults to the identity operator, so the following creates the same dataset:

dataset = FunctionalDataset(blocks=[
    ObservationBlock.from_arrays(
        points=points,
        y=readings,
        variance=0.01,
        name="observed_values",
        max_size=points.shape[0],
    )
])

variance specifies the measurement-error variance shared by the block. Here max_size=points.shape[0] reserves exactly the three locations in this fixed dataset. Observation capacity explains reserving space for a growing experiment.

docs.title: Construct a query
docs.text:
Queries have the same location/operator structure but no observations or noise. Block names become keys in the result.

jnp.linspace returns a one-dimensional array of shape (101,). The [:, None] below adds a column axis, giving the required (101, 1) locations.

from gpex import FunctionalBlock, FunctionalQuery, operators

x = jnp.linspace(-1.5, 1.5, 101)[:, None]
query = FunctionalQuery([
    FunctionalBlock(x, operators.Identity(), "value"),
    FunctionalBlock(x, operators.Gradient(), "gradient"),
])

docs.title: Condition and predict
docs.text:
from gpex import GaussianProcess, kernels

gp = GaussianProcess(kernels.RBFKernel(variance=1.0, lengthscale=0.7))
posterior = gp.condition(dataset)
prediction = posterior.predict_marginals(query)

prediction.mean["value"]          # shape (101,)
prediction.mean["gradient"]       # shape (101, 1)
prediction.variance["value"]      # shape (101,)
prediction.variance["gradient"]   # shape (101, 1)

predict_marginals computes the mean and variance at each query output without building a full query covariance. When you need correlations between outputs, request a joint prediction explicitly:

joint = posterior.predict(query)
joint.covariance.full                    # shape (202, 202)
joint.covariance.block("value", "gradient")  # shape (101, 101, 1)

To use a Matérn kernel or a lengthscale per coordinate, see Kernels and means.

Continue with First posterior, or read Observations, designs, and queries for the underlying block model. To train kernel or observation-noise parameters, see Fitting hyperparameters.

docs.title: Numerical backends
docs.text: GaussianProcess accepts a numerical backend through solver. linalg.DenseBackend() is the stateless default backend. Its prepare method returns a CholeskySystem containing the factorization and activity state for exact dense inference and fitting.

docs.title: Backend contract
docs.text:
SolverConfiguration.prepare(system, ...) prepares an immutable LinearSystem. The input SymmetricLinearOperator supplies capacity, matmul, diagonal, and tiled materialize. Prepared systems provide solves, quadratic forms, log determinants, covariance and variance reductions, reusable projections, and append operations. These interfaces use numerical arrays and activity information rather than GP measurement types.

For a prepared system, size is the active scalar count as a dynamic JAX integer, and capacity is the reserved scalar dimension as a static Python integer. Solves and projections accept full-capacity inputs. Activation increases size while preserving capacity. Input operators also expose capacity, and updates expose previous_capacity for the reserved dimension before activation.

Custom backends inherit from eqx.Module and SolverConfiguration. Their prepared systems inherit from eqx.Module and LinearSystem. Both interfaces are abstract base classes, so subclasses must implement all abstract methods before they can be instantiated. Numerical inputs and update descriptions explicitly inherit the SymmetricLinearOperator and LinearSystemUpdate abstract base classes. Updates store their numerical system and newly active indices as fields.

The small input interface keeps backends independent of kernels and observation types. Dense preparation requests materialization. The operator also supports products without storing the full matrix, ready for future iterative backends.

CovarianceProjection is an abstract interface for reusable covariance reductions. The dense CholeskyProjection stores a whitened cross-covariance whose Gram matrix is the reduction. Diagonal and cross reductions let consumers reuse that state without accessing a backend's factorization.

Likelihood objectives use the configured backend's quadratic_form and logdet. The dense quadratic form needs one triangular solve. Invalid factorizations propagate non-finite statistics so fitting can reject invalid trials. Backend configuration, prepared state, and returned results must support JAX transformations, with numerical arrays stored as dynamic PyTree leaves.

Use configuration.prepare(system) to construct prepared state. For an already materialized matrix, use CholeskySystem.from_matrix(matrix, jitter=...). Factorization uses the symmetric part of the matrix with diagonal jitter. cholops owns this input symmetrization and the symmetry-preserving reverse rule.

Dense systems store a cholops PaddedCholesky in factor. cholops owns factorization, numerical consumers, reserved-slot activation, and coefficient reuse. factor.order maps physical factor rows to canonical slots, and factor.inverse_order maps canonical slots back to physical rows. factor.factor exposes the lower-triangular array in physical order. solve and project accept canonical-order inputs. Preparing a system with active=mask reserves the inactive identity slots for append. Solves, quadratic forms, and projections ignore inactive input entries, including non-finite values. Solves return zero inactive coefficients. Generic systems without a mask are fully active. CholeskySystem(factor, tile_size) wraps an existing PaddedCholesky.

Jitter is owned by the input system. Preparation returns a reusable :class:CholeskySystem containing the factorization and activity state.

docs.title: prepare
docs.text:
prepare(
    system: SymmetricLinearOperator,
    *,
    materialization_tile_size: int | None = None,
    active: Activity | None = None,
) -> CholeskySystem

Prepare a factorization from a backend-neutral operator.

If supplied, active identifies used rows. Inactive rows must be an independent identity system. They become reusable factor storage. Numerical consumers ignore inactive input entries. If no activity mask is supplied, every row is active.

Source code in src/gpex/linalg/dense.py 
def prepare(
    self,
    system: SymmetricLinearOperator,
    *,
    materialization_tile_size: int | None = None,
    active: Activity | None = None,
) -> CholeskySystem:
    """Prepare a factorization from a backend-neutral operator.

    If supplied, ``active`` identifies used rows. Inactive rows must be an
    independent identity system. They become reusable factor storage.
    Numerical consumers ignore inactive input entries. If no activity
    mask is supplied, every row is active.
    """
    matrix = system.materialize(tile_size=materialization_tile_size)
    if active is None:
        active = jnp.ones(system.capacity, dtype=bool)
    factor = PaddedCholesky.from_matrix(matrix, active=active)
    return CholeskySystem(factor, materialization_tile_size)

Source code in src/gpex/linalg/dense.py 
@classmethod
def from_matrix(cls, matrix: SquareMatrix, jitter: float) -> CholeskySystem:
    """Factorize the symmetric part of a square matrix with diagonal jitter."""
    validate_jitter(jitter)
    matrix = jnp.asarray(matrix)
    if matrix.ndim != 2 or matrix.shape[0] != matrix.shape[1]:
        raise ValueError("matrix must be square")
    stabilized = matrix + jitter * jnp.eye(matrix.shape[0])
    factor = PaddedCholesky.from_matrix(
        stabilized, active=jnp.ones(matrix.shape[0], dtype=bool)
    )
    return cls(factor, None)

docs.title: solve
docs.text:
solve(right_hand_side: RightHandSide) -> RightHandSide

Solve on active rows for vector or array RHS, including empty batches.

Inactive input entries are ignored and inactive solution entries are zero.

Source code in src/gpex/linalg/dense.py 
def solve(
    self,
    right_hand_side: RightHandSide,
) -> RightHandSide:
    """Solve on active rows for vector or array RHS, including empty batches.

    Inactive input entries are ignored and inactive solution entries are zero.
    """
    right_hand_side = jnp.asarray(right_hand_side)
    if right_hand_side.ndim == 0 or right_hand_side.shape[0] != self.capacity:
        raise ValueError("right-hand side must start with the system capacity")
    shape = right_hand_side.shape
    columns = right_hand_side.reshape((self.capacity, -1))
    return self.factor.solve(columns).reshape(shape)

docs.title: quadratic_form
docs.text:
quadratic_form(right_hand_side: Vector) -> Scalar

Return the active inverse quadratic form with one triangular solve.

The vector has shape (capacity,) in canonical order. Supports JIT, vectorization, and differentiation through the factor and vector. Inactive entries are ignored. Failed factorizations propagate non-finite values on the active system.

Source code in src/gpex/linalg/dense.py 
def quadratic_form(self, right_hand_side: Vector) -> Scalar:
    """Return the active inverse quadratic form with one triangular solve.

    The vector has shape ``(capacity,)`` in canonical order. Supports JIT,
    vectorization, and differentiation through the factor and vector.
    Inactive entries are ignored. Failed factorizations propagate non-finite
    values on the active system.
    """
    right_hand_side = jnp.asarray(right_hand_side)
    if right_hand_side.shape != (self.capacity,):
        raise ValueError(
            "right-hand side must be a vector with the system capacity"
        )
    return self.factor.quadratic(right_hand_side)

Activate reserved slots with a Schur-complement factor update.

Source code in src/gpex/linalg/dense.py 
def append(self, update: LinearSystemUpdate) -> CholeskySystem:
    """Activate reserved slots with a Schur-complement factor update."""
    cross, appended_covariance = self._trailing_blocks(update)
    with jax.default_matmul_precision("highest"):
        factor = self.factor.activate(update.indices, cross, appended_covariance)
    return eqx.tree_at(lambda s: s.factor, self, factor)

    update: LinearSystemUpdate,
    solution: Vector,
    right_hand_side: Vector,

            rhs=right_hand_side,

Apply latent covariance to canonical rows without constructing its matrix.

Accept vectors or arrays with leading dimension equal to the scalar functional size. Inactive inputs are ignored and inactive outputs are zero. One operator output is indivisible and can exceed tile_size. Pairwise tiles are recomputed in reverse mode, bounding working storage in both directions. Supports JIT, vmap, and differentiation of numerical inputs. General kernels still require quadratic pairwise work per application.

def apply_covariance(
    blocks: Functionals,
    kernel: ScalarKernel,
    right_hand_side: FunctionalColumns,
    *,
    tile_size: int = 128,
) -> FunctionalColumns:
    """Apply latent covariance to canonical rows without constructing its matrix.

    Accept vectors or arrays with leading dimension equal to the scalar
    functional size. Inactive inputs are ignored and inactive outputs are zero.
    One operator output is indivisible and can exceed ``tile_size``. Pairwise
    tiles are recomputed in reverse mode, bounding working storage in both
    directions. Supports JIT, vmap, and differentiation of numerical inputs.
    General kernels still require quadratic pairwise work per application.
    """
    _validate_tile_size(tile_size)
    measurements = prepare_functionals(blocks)
    _validate_kernel_compatibility((measurements,), kernel)
    right_hand_side = jnp.asarray(right_hand_side)
    if right_hand_side.ndim == 0 or right_hand_side.shape[0] != measurements.size:
        raise ValueError("right-hand side must start with the functional size")
    shape = right_hand_side.shape
    columns = measurements.to_grouped(measurements.mask(right_hand_side)).reshape(
        (measurements.size, prod(shape[1:]))
    )
    layouts = tuple(
        _TileLayout.from_group(group, tile_size) for group in measurements.groups
    )
    inputs = []
    start = 0
    for layout in layouts:
        inputs.append(
            jnp.pad(
                columns[start : start + layout.size],
                ((0, layout.padded_size - layout.size), (0, 0)),
            )
        )
        start += layout.size
    parts = []
    for left in layouts:
        product = jnp.zeros((left.size, columns.shape[1]))
        for right, values in zip(layouts, inputs, strict=True):
            product = product + _apply_group_covariance(left, right, kernel, values)
        parts.append(product)
    result = measurements.to_canonical(jnp.concatenate(parts))
    return measurements.mask(result).reshape(shape)

    """Apply each functional to the mean and return canonical scalar ordering.

    Accept public blocks or prepared groups. Inactive reserved entries are zero.
    Supports JIT, vmap, and differentiation of numerical inputs.

    def scalar_mean(point: Point) -> Scalar:

            raise ValueError("mean functions must return a scalar")

    parts = [

            group.operators, group.points
        ).reshape(-1)
        for group in measurements.groups
    ]
    return measurements.mask(measurements.to_canonical(jnp.concatenate(parts)))

def assemble_covariance(
    left_blocks: Functionals,
    right_blocks: Functionals,
    kernel: ScalarKernel,
    *,
    tile_size: int | None = None,
) -> FlatCovariance:
    """Materialize covariance, optionally bounding pairwise working tiles.

    Tiles traverse numerical operator groups rather than public blocks. One
    operator output is never split. The final dense matrix is still allocated.
    With ``None``, each complete group pair is vectorized.
    """
    if tile_size is not None:
        _validate_tile_size(tile_size)
    left, right = prepare_functionals(left_blocks), prepare_functionals(right_blocks)
    if left.input_dimension != right.input_dimension:
        raise ValueError("covariance blocks must use the same input dimension")
    _validate_kernel_compatibility((left, right), kernel)
    rows = []
    for group in left.groups:
        row = jnp.concatenate(
            [
                _assemble_group_covariance(group, other, kernel, tile_size=tile_size)
                for other in right.groups
            ],
            axis=1,
        )
        if len(left.groups) > 1 or len(right.groups) > 1:
            # TODO: Remove this temporary compiler/driver workaround once the
            # mixed CUDA regression passes without it on the fixed toolchain.
            # JAX/jaxlib 0.10.2 on H100 with NVIDIA 615.71.09 can raise an illegal
            # address when fusing values/slopes/averages covariance assembly.
            # Separate completed rows from the final join. Barriers on each
            # individual pair instead expose another failure at smaller sizes.
            row = jax.lax.optimization_barrier(row)
        rows.append(row)
    covariance = left.to_canonical(jnp.concatenate(rows, axis=0))
    return left.mask(right.mask(right.to_canonical(covariance.T)).T)

def assemble_covariance_diagonal(
    blocks: Functionals, kernel: ScalarKernel
) -> FlatVector:
    """Assemble the prior diagonal without allocating a full covariance."""
    measurements = prepare_functionals(blocks)
    _validate_kernel_compatibility((measurements,), kernel)
    parts = []
    for group in measurements.groups:
        components = prod(group.output_shape)

        def point_diagonal(operator, point, components=components):
            covariance = operator_covariance(
                kernel, operator, operator, x=point, y=point
            )
            return jnp.diag(covariance.reshape((components, components)))

        parts.append(
            eqx.filter_vmap(point_diagonal)(group.operators, group.points).reshape(-1)
        )
    return measurements.mask(measurements.to_canonical(jnp.concatenate(parts)))

CovarianceSystem describes an observation covariance including block noise, jitter, and reserved inactive slots. Backends can consume it through the SymmetricLinearOperator interface:

product = system.matmul(rhs, tile_size=128)
diagonal = system.diagonal()

Products support JIT, vmap, and numerical differentiation. Pairwise intermediates are recomputed in reverse mode so differentiation also avoids full covariance storage. def matmul(
    self, right_hand_side: RightHandSide, *, tile_size: int = 128
) -> RightHandSide:
    """Apply covariance, noise, and jitter using bounded pairwise tiles.

    Inputs have shape ``(capacity, *columns)`` in canonical order. Inactive
    slots act as independent identity rows, unlike a prepared solve which
    ignores inactive inputs. Supports JIT, vmap, and differentiation.
    """
    right_hand_side = jnp.asarray(right_hand_side)
    covariance_product = apply_covariance(
        self.measurements, self.kernel, right_hand_side, tile_size=tile_size
    )
    shift = self.diagonal_shift().reshape(
        (-1,) + (1,) * (right_hand_side.ndim - 1)
    )
    return covariance_product + shift * right_hand_side

def __init__(
    self,
    functional: FunctionalBlock,
    variance: PositiveParameter | Scalar | float,
    *,
    max_size: int | None = None,
    count: Count | int | None = None,
) -> None:
    if isinstance(variance, PositiveParameter):
        value = variance.value
    else:
        variance = jnp.asarray(variance)
        variance = error_if(
            variance,
            jnp.any(~jnp.isfinite(variance) | (variance < 0)),
            "noise variances must be finite and nonnegative",
        )
        value = variance
    if value.ndim != 0:
        raise ValueError("noise variance must be scalar")
    supplied = functional.locations.count
    capacity = max(1024, supplied) if max_size is None else max_size
    if isinstance(capacity, bool) or not isinstance(capacity, int):
        raise TypeError("max_size must be an integer")
    if capacity < supplied:
        raise ValueError("max_size must be at least the supplied location count")
    count = jnp.asarray(supplied if count is None else count)
    if count.ndim != 0 or not jnp.issubdtype(count.dtype, jnp.integer):
        raise ValueError("active count must be an integer scalar")
    count = error_if(
        count,
        (count < 0) | (count > supplied),
        "active count must lie within the supplied locations",
    )
    points = jnp.pad(
        functional.locations.points,
        ((0, capacity - supplied), (0, 0)),
        mode="edge",
    )
    points = jnp.where((jnp.arange(capacity) < count)[:, None], points, points[0])
    self.functional = eqx.tree_at(lambda f: f.locations.points, functional, points)
    self.variance = variance
    self.count = count

def append(self, locations: Locations) -> ObservationDesignBlock:
    """Fill unused locations, retaining operator, name, variance and capacity.

    Locations have shape ``(m, d)`` with the existing input dimension ``d``.
    The returned design supports JIT and differentiation.
    """
    if locations.input_dimension != self.functional.locations.input_dimension:
        raise ValueError("appended locations must have the same input dimension")
    if locations.count > self.capacity:
        raise ValueError("appended locations exceed max_size")
    points, count = error_if(
        (self.functional.locations.points, self.count),
        self.count + locations.count > self.capacity,
        "appended locations exceed max_size",
    )
    points = jax.lax.dynamic_update_slice_in_dim(
        points, locations.points, count, axis=0
    )
    count = count + locations.count
    points = jnp.where(
        (jnp.arange(self.capacity) < count)[:, None], points, points[0]
    )
    return eqx.tree_at(
        lambda b: (b.functional.locations.points, b.count), self, (points, count)
    )

def replace(self, points: Points) -> ObservationDesignBlock:
    """Replace all active locations, preserving capacity and shared variance.

    Empty contents retain the previous valid padding point. Supports JIT
    and differentiation. Different input shapes specialize this operation,
    but its result always has the original reserved shapes.
    """
    points = jnp.asarray(points)
    expected = self.functional.locations.input_dimension
    if points.ndim != 2 or points.shape[1] != expected:
        raise ValueError(f"replacement locations must have shape (n, {expected})")
    count = points.shape[0]
    if count > self.capacity:
        raise ValueError("replacement locations exceed max_size")
    if count == 0:
        points = self.functional.locations.points[:1]
    functional = FunctionalBlock(
        points, self.functional.operator, self.functional.name
    )
    return ObservationDesignBlock(
        functional, self.variance, max_size=self.capacity, count=count
    )

@classmethod
def from_arrays(
    cls,
    points: Points,
    y: FunctionalValues,
    *,
    variance: PositiveParameter | Scalar | float,
    name: str,
    operator: LinearOperator | None = None,
    max_size: int | None = None,
    padding_point: Point | None = None,
) -> ObservationBlock:
    """Construct observations directly from coordinates and outcomes.

    ``points`` has shape ``(n, d)``. The default identity operator expects
    ``y`` of shape ``(n,)``; otherwise use ``(n, *operator.output_shape(d))``.
    ``variance`` is one scalar measurement-error variance shared by the block.
    Numerical values may be traced; the name and shapes must remain static.

    ``max_size`` reserves locations, defaulting to ``max(1024, n)``.
    Unused slots repeat the first point. For ``n=0``, supply a
    ``padding_point`` valid for the kernel, mean and operator, and an array
    ``points`` with shape ``(0, d)``. Padding is excluded from inference.
    """
    operator = Identity() if operator is None else operator
    points = jnp.asarray(points)
    if points.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError("locations must have shape (n, d)")
    count = points.shape[0]
    if count == 0:
        if padding_point is None:
            raise ValueError("empty observations require a valid padding_point")
        padding_point = jnp.asarray(padding_point)
        if padding_point.shape != (points.shape[1],):
            raise ValueError("padding_point must match the input dimension")
        points = padding_point[None, :]
    return cls(
        ObservationDesignBlock(
            FunctionalBlock(points, operator, name),
            variance,
            max_size=max_size,
            count=count,
        ),
        y,
    )

    """Append outcomes using this block's operator and shared variance.

    Locations have shape ``(m, d)`` with the existing input dimension ``d``;

def pack(self, values: Mapping[str, FunctionalValues]) -> FlatValues:
    extra = set(values) - {block.name for block in self.blocks}
    if extra:
        raise ValueError(f"unexpected blocks: {sorted(extra)}")
    parts = []
    for block in self.blocks:
        value = jnp.asarray(values[block.name])
        if value.shape != block.shape:
            raise ValueError(
                f"block {block.name!r} has shape {value.shape}; "
                f"expected {block.shape}"
            )
        parts.append(value.reshape(-1))
    return jnp.concatenate(parts)

    fit_one: Callable[[Model], FitResult[Model]],
) -> MultiStartFitResult[Model]:
    """Vectorize a fitting callable over informed parameter starts.

    For example, ``fit_multistart(starts, lambda m: fit_lbfgs(m, objective))``.
    Starts may differ only in their explicit parameter arrays: structure,
    shapes, parameter metadata, and fixed leaves must agree. Each run owns its
    optimizer state. Any failed run raises; finite final objectives determine
    the selected model. This function selects ``best_index`` on the host; use
    the single-fit functions when nesting fitting inside another JIT.
    """
    runs, models = _map_starts(starts, fit_one)
    return MultiStartFitResult(
        models=models,
        losses=runs.losses,
        optimizer_state=runs.optimizer_state,
        final_losses=runs.loss,
        gradient_norms=runs.gradient_norm,
        step_counts=runs.step_count,
        evaluation_counts=runs.evaluation_count,
        converged=runs.converged,
        best_index=int(jax.device_get(jnp.argmin(runs.loss))),
    )

docs.text:
fit_random_subsets draws a fresh subset without replacement from each observation block at every Optax update. An integer subset_size applies to every block, or a mapping gives counts by block name. All output components at a selected location stay together, along with the block's shared noise. Each selected count must be between one and the active location count.

A GP marginal likelihood couples observations through its covariance. A subset objective is therefore an approximation, even after likelihood scaling. For MAP, scale only the likelihood and include the prior once. Use a full-data reference_objective to evaluate the final model. The subset fitting example shows the complete objective and its scaling.

subset_losses records each update's proxy objective. Values from different subsets are not directly comparable. reference_loss is evaluated once at the final model. Multistart subset fits select by their final full-data reference_losses. Use a first-order Optax optimizer for the changing subset objective.

def fit_multistart_random_subsets(
    starts: Sequence[GPModel],
    subset_objective: Objective[GPModel],
    optimizer: optax.GradientTransformation,
    *,
    step_count: int,
    subset_size: SubsetSize,
    reference_objective: Objective[GPModel],
    key: PRNGKeyArray,
) -> MultiStartRandomSubsetFitResult[GPModel]:
    """Run ``fit_random_subsets`` with an independent key per start.

    Arguments and failure behavior match ``fit_random_subsets``. Starts must
    satisfy the same structure and fixed-leaf requirements as ``fit_multistart``.
    Select the final model with the lowest full-data reference objective.
    """
    keys = jax.random.split(key, len(starts))

    def fit_one(model: GPModel, start_key: PRNGKeyArray):
        return fit_random_subsets(
            model,
            subset_objective,
            optimizer,
            step_count=step_count,
            subset_size=subset_size,
            reference_objective=reference_objective,
            key=start_key,
        )

    runs, models = _map_starts(starts, fit_one, keys)
    return MultiStartRandomSubsetFitResult(
        models=models,
        subset_losses=runs.subset_losses,
        optimizer_state=runs.optimizer_state,
        reference_losses=runs.reference_loss,
        reference_gradient_norms=runs.reference_gradient_norm,
        step_counts=runs.step_count,

def negative_log_marginal_likelihood(
    gp: GaussianProcess,
    dataset: FunctionalDataset,
    *,
    jitter: float = 1e-6,
) -> ScalarObjective:
    """Return the exact Gaussian negative log marginal likelihood.

    Invalid factorizations produce non-finite trials for optimizers to reject.
    Padding contributes neither observations nor likelihood normalization.
    """
    measurements = prepare_functionals(tuple(block.design for block in dataset.blocks))
    variance = dataset.variance_flat
    system = CovarianceSystem(measurements, gp.kernel, variance, jitter)
    prepared = gp.solver.prepare(
        system,
        materialization_tile_size=gp.covariance_tile_size,
        active=measurements.active,
    )
    residual = dataset.values_flat - assemble_mean(measurements, gp.mean)
    quadratic = prepared.quadratic_form(residual)
    logdet = prepared.logdet()
    normalizer = dataset.active_size * jnp.log(2 * jnp.pi)
    return 0.5 * (quadratic + logdet + normalizer)

docs.title: Conditioning and numerical options
docs.text:
gp.condition(dataset, jitter=1e-6) adds jitter to the observation covariance diagonal before solving. Jitter is an absolute covariance quantity and must be finite and nonnegative. Choose it in the units of your model and keep it consistent between fitting and conditioning. Observation noise is specified by the dataset's design. Sampling has its own jitter argument for stabilizing the query covariance factorization.

The default dense solver supports first-order forward and reverse derivatives through conditioning and updates. Higher-order derivatives through its factorization and updates are unsupported. Failed Cholesky factorizations can produce non-finite results, including under JIT. Check outputs before using them. Use consistent floating precision, sensible units, and explicit regularization for redundant measurements. A jitter too small relative to the covariance diagonal can round away.

GaussianProcess(kernel, covariance_tile_size=1024) evaluates observation covariances in smaller tiles. Tile size counts scalar outputs, with at least one location's complete output per tile. Smaller tiles reduce temporary memory at the cost of more loop overhead. The final dense covariance and its factorization still have to fit in memory. The default is None. See numerical backends for solver configuration and interfaces.

docs.title: Proposed measurements and posterior updates
docs.text:
gp.prepare_conditioning(design) returns a ConditioningState for covariance calculations before outcomes are available. PreparedQuery(conditioning, query) reuses a fixed target when comparing proposed measurements. Preparation stores the full target covariance, including for subsequent variance-only requests. Rebuild it after changing the GP, existing design, jitter, or target.

posterior.append(locations, readings, block="name") updates an existing posterior within a declared block's capacity. posterior.conditioning.append performs a covariance update without readings. See Experimental design and Sequential observations for their use, and observation capacity for compilation and model-reuse conditions.

    design: ObservationDesign | FunctionalDataset,
    *,
    jitter: float = 1e-6,

        system,
        linear_system,
        design.index_map,

def condition(
    self, dataset: FunctionalDataset, *, jitter: float = 1e-6
) -> ConditionedPosterior[KernelType]:
    """Condition on a dataset with ``gp.condition(dataset, jitter=1e-6)``.

    The callable captures this immutable GP and can be compiled directly:
    ``condition = eqx.filter_jit(gp.condition)``. Reuse it across datasets
    with the same reserved block structure and dtypes. Values, locations,
    noise and active counts may change without compiling again. To change
    or differentiate model parameters, pass the GP into a compiled function.

    Returns a posterior for the current contents on every call. This does
    not reuse a previous factorization. Dense work scales with the reserved
    scalar capacity, including unused slots.

    Args:
        dataset: Named observation blocks with reserved locations, observed
            operator outputs, active counts and scalar noise variances.
        jitter: Diagonal stabilization of the observation covariance.
            Defaults to ``1e-6``. Unused slots retain a unit diagonal.

    Returns:
        A posterior supporting prediction and sampling. Failed dense
            factorization propagates non-finite numerical results.
    """
    conditioning = self.prepare_conditioning(dataset, jitter=jitter)
    observation_mean = assemble_mean(conditioning.measurements, self.mean)
    values = dataset.values_flat
    alpha = conditioning.solve(values - observation_mean)
    return ConditionedPosterior(conditioning, values, alpha)

def append_solve(
    self,
    locations: Locations,
    solution: ObservationVector,
    right_hand_side: ObservationVector,
    *,
    block: str,
) -> tuple[ConditioningState[KernelType], ObservationVector]:
    """Activate locations and update a canonical-order vector solution.

    RHS must retain all existing active entries and be zero in unused slots.
    Dense updates reuse the factor and update the existing coefficients.

        self.gp, update.system, linear_system, self.index_map, self.block_layout
    )
    return conditioning, updated_solution

    can cross an outer ``jit`` or ``vmap`` boundary. Storage includes the
    observation/query cross-covariance, but no full query covariance.

def predict(self, query: FunctionalQuery) -> Prediction:
    """Return the joint latent mean and covariance at a query.

    Args:
        query: Named blocks of locations and linear operators to predict.

    Returns:
        A ``Prediction`` with structured means and a full ``(q, q)`` covariance for
            ``q`` flattened query outputs. The complete result is a PyTree and can
            be returned from JIT-compiled functions.
    """
    conditioning = self.conditioning
    gp = conditioning.gp
    cross = _assemble_query_cross(conditioning, query)
    prior_mean = assemble_mean(query.blocks, gp.mean)
    mean = StructuredValues(
        prior_mean
        + jnp.matmul(cross.T, self.alpha, precision=jax.lax.Precision.HIGHEST),
        query.index_map,
    )
    prior_covariance = assemble_covariance(
        query.blocks,
        query.blocks,
        gp.kernel,
        tile_size=gp.covariance_tile_size,
    )
    covariance = symmetrize(
        prior_covariance - conditioning.linear_system.covariance_reduction(cross)
    )
    return Prediction(mean, CovarianceResult(covariance, query.index_map))

def append(
    self,
    locations: Locations,
    values: FunctionalValues,
    *,
    block: str,
) -> ConditionedPosterior[KernelType]:
    """Add observations to a declared block without enlarging storage.

    ``locations`` has shape ``(m, d)``. ``values`` has shape
    ``(m, *operator_output_shape)`` for the selected block. Its operator,
    noise variance, model parameters and previous observations remain fixed.
    Returns a new posterior; overflow raises instead of resizing.

    Repeated fixed-shape batches into the same block reuse an outer JIT.
    Dense systems update their factor and coefficients through the Schur
    complement.
    """
    index = self.conditioning.index_map.block(block)
    values = jnp.asarray(values)
    expected = (locations.count, *index.shape[1:])
    if values.shape != expected:
        raise ValueError(
            f"appended values have shape {values.shape}; expected {expected}"
        )
    update = self.conditioning._prepare_update(locations, block=block)
    y_flat = self.y_flat.at[update.indices].set(values.reshape(-1))
    right_hand_side = y_flat - assemble_mean(
        update.system.measurements, self.conditioning.gp.mean
    )
    linear_system, alpha = self.conditioning.linear_system.append_solve(
        update, self.alpha, right_hand_side
    )
    conditioning = ConditioningState(
        self.conditioning.gp,
        update.system,
        linear_system,
        self.conditioning.index_map,
        self.conditioning.block_layout,
    )
    return ConditionedPosterior(conditioning, y_flat, alpha)

def block(self, left_name: str, right_name: str) -> CovarianceBlock:
    """Return a named cross-covariance with shape ``(*left.shape, *right.shape)``.

    Args:
        left_name: Row block name from the query.
        right_name: Column block name from the query.

            Leading batch axes introduced by ``vmap`` are preserved too.

    left = self.index_map.block(left_name)
    right = self.index_map.block(right_name)
    leading_shape = self.full.shape[:-2]
    return self.full[..., left.slice, right.slice].reshape(

The path uses the kernel's random features for the prior and a pathwise conditioning correction for the observations. Repeated calls evaluate the same draw, so the object can be vectorized, differentiated, or passed to a LinearOperator. Construct with FeaturePosteriorPath(posterior, key). For exact samples at a fixed finite query, use posterior.sample(key, query). Differentiating a finite feature expansion beyond the GP's smoothness does not define a valid GP derivative.

def __init__(
    self,
    posterior: ConditionedPosterior[KernelType],
    key: PRNGKeyArray,
    *,
    feature_count: int = 1024,
) -> None:
    conditioning = posterior.conditioning
    kernel = conditioning.gp.kernel
    if not isinstance(kernel, FeatureKernel):
        raise TypeError(
            "FeaturePosteriorPath requires a FeatureKernel; "
            f"got {type(kernel).__name__}. "
            "Use posterior.sample(key, query) for finite-query samples."
        )
    input_dimension = conditioning.measurements.input_dimension
    feature_key, weight_key, noise_key = jax.random.split(key, 3)
    features = kernel.random_features(
        feature_key, input_dimension, feature_count=feature_count
    )
    prior_path = _FeaturePath(
        features=features,
        weights=jax.random.normal(weight_key, (feature_count,)),
    )

    self.prior_path = prior_path
    self.mean = conditioning.gp.mean
    self.kernel = kernel
    self.measurements = conditioning.measurements
    self.correction_weights = _conditioning_weights(
        posterior, prior_path, noise_key
    )
    self.covariance_tile_size = conditioning.gp.covariance_tile_size
    self.input_dimension = input_dimension

docs.title: Built-in kernel families
docs.text:
Standard kernels accept variance=1.0 and lengthscale=1.0 by default. variance is the covariance amplitude. A scalar lengthscale gives isotropic scaling, and a vector supplies one lengthscale per input coordinate (ARD).

import jax.numpy as jnp
from gpex.kernels import RBFKernel, Matern52Kernel

isotropic = RBFKernel(variance=1.0, lengthscale=0.7)
ard = Matern52Kernel(variance=1.0, lengthscale=jnp.array([0.7, 1.2]))
Class Kernel family Supported GP derivative order Matern12Kernel Matérn, ν = 1/2 0 Matern32Kernel Matérn, ν = 3/2 1 Matern52Kernel Matérn, ν = 5/2 2 RBFKernel Squared exponential Any finite order

All four families support callable posterior paths. Kernel sums and products, constructed with + and *, support conditioning, prediction, and finite-query sampling. They do not currently provide features for callable paths.

docs.title: Full input metrics
docs.text:
The Generalized...Kernel variants of these four families accept a complete lower-triangular factor L with a positive diagonal. It defines the precision metric M = L @ L.T, with distance norm(L.T @ (x - y)):

from gpex.kernels import GeneralizedMatern52Kernel

L = jnp.array([[1.4, 0.0], [0.3, 0.8]])
kernel = GeneralizedMatern52Kernel(variance=1.0, L=L)

For a diagonal L, its diagonal entries are reciprocal lengthscales. L = jnp.diag(1 / jnp.array([0.7, 1.2])) reproduces the corresponding ARD metric. Generalized kernels also support callable paths.

Plain numbers and arrays remain fixed during fitting. Use PositiveParameter for variance and lengthscales, or CholeskyParameter for L, to make them trainable. Read values through kernel.variance, kernel.lengthscales.lengthscale, or kernel.lengthscales.L. See Fitting hyperparameters and parameters and priors.

docs.title: Compose kernels and means
docs.text:
Use + and * to compose kernels or means. For example, this two-dimensional model combines a trainable full input metric with a product of two fixed RBF kernels and a linear mean:

from gpex import GaussianProcess
from gpex.kernels import GeneralizedRBFKernel
from gpex.means import ConstantMean, LinearMean
from gpex.parameters import CholeskyParameter
from gpex.parameters.priors import IndependentCholeskyPrior, LogNormalPrior, NormalPrior

factor = CholeskyParameter(
    jnp.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.2, 1.4]]),
    prior=IndependentCholeskyPrior(
        diagonal_prior=LogNormalPrior(log_standard_deviation=0.5),
        off_diagonal_prior=NormalPrior(standard_deviation=0.4),
    ),
    name="precision_factor",
)
local = GeneralizedRBFKernel(variance=1.0, L=factor)
broad = RBFKernel(variance=0.3, lengthscale=2.0)
modulation = RBFKernel(lengthscale=jnp.array([1.5, 0.8]))
mean = LinearMean(weights=jnp.array([0.15, -0.1])) + ConstantMean(0.2)

docs.title: Extension interfaces
docs.text:
A Kernel maps two points of shape (d,) to a scalar covariance. A Mean maps one point to a scalar mean. Both are Equinox modules. Custom kernels must be positive semidefinite and declare max_derivative_order when the latent GP has finite smoothness. Evaluation must support the JAX transformations required by the chosen operators, including derivatives at coincident inputs.

RadialKernel supplies input scaling and evaluation from squared distance. Subclasses define _correlation and _derivative_order. RadialFeatureKernel also requires _sample_frequencies for its unit-scale correlation.

SeparableKernel.factorization(input_dimension) returns a KernelFactorization(coefficient, factors). Each factor is a scalar-coordinate kernel, and their product times the coefficient must equal the kernel and its derivatives. Derive factors from current parameter values. Factors with array state should be Equinox modules. This interface enables factored tensor quadrature. Pass the kernel object directly to GaussianProcess to expose this capability.

FeatureKernel.random_features returns a fixed callable mapping one point to a feature vector. Feature inner products approximate the complete kernel, including its variance. Store random draws as array fields so repeated calls use the same features and the map can cross JIT boundaries. Exact finite feature maps are supported as well. See the class contracts below.

def random_features(
    self,
    key: PRNGKeyArray,
    input_dimension: int,
    *,
    feature_count: int = 1024,
) -> Callable[[Point], Array]:
    """Construct Fourier features; see
    [`FeatureKernel.random_features`][gpex.kernels.FeatureKernel.random_features].
    """
    if (
        isinstance(feature_count, bool)
        or not isinstance(feature_count, int)
        or feature_count < 1
    ):
        raise ValueError("feature_count must be a positive integer")
    if (
        isinstance(input_dimension, bool)
        or not isinstance(input_dimension, int)
        or input_dimension < 1
    ):
        raise ValueError("input_dimension must be a positive integer")
    self.lengthscales.validate_dimension(input_dimension)
    frequency_key, phase_key = jax.random.split(key)
    frequencies = self.lengthscales.transform_frequencies(
        self._sample_frequencies(frequency_key, (feature_count, input_dimension))
    )
    phases = jax.random.uniform(
        phase_key, (feature_count,), minval=0.0, maxval=2.0 * jnp.pi
    )
    return _FourierFeatures(
        frequencies, phases, jnp.sqrt(2.0 * self.variance / feature_count)
    )

docs.title: Custom operators
docs.text:
A LinearOperator implements output_shape(input_dimension) and apply(function, point). The point has shape (d,). For a scalar function, apply must return the declared output shape. It must also preserve any output axes already present on the supplied function, because covariance construction applies operators to both kernel arguments.

The operation must be linear in function. Its locations, weights, and other parameters must be independent of the function's values. Use JAX-compatible operations for jit, vmap, and differentiation. Store differentiable numerical parameters as array fields. Structural settings such as quadrature order can be static Equinox fields.

The default derivative_order is zero. Override it when the operator takes derivatives of the function. gpex checks it against the kernel's supported GP derivative order. A finite difference made from function evaluations has order zero under this contract.

docs.title: Quadrature interfaces
docs.text:
QuadratureOperator.quadrature(point) returns absolute evaluation points with shape (q, d) and weights with shape (q,). Its inherited apply evaluates and weights the function while preserving existing output axes. The default scalar output_shape may be overridden for input-dimension restrictions.

Weights may be negative and need not sum to one. Include normalization and change-of-variable factors in the rule. Points and weights may depend on the query location and operator parameters. Keep the number of nodes fixed under tracing.

TensorQuadratureOperator.coordinate_quadrature(point) returns one (nodes, weights) pair per coordinate in input order. Each array is one-dimensional. Node counts can differ between coordinates and must remain fixed under tracing. The full weight is the product of the coordinate weights. Any override of quadrature or apply must represent that same product rule. This interface enables efficient covariance evaluation with SeparableKernel.

docs.title: Built-in constructors and methods
docs.text: Identity(), Gradient(), Hessian(), and Laplacian() are stateless. PartialDerivative(axis) selects one coordinate axis, which is static under JAX transformations. Numerical directions, displacements, radii, and smoothing scales are dynamic array parameters.

docs.title: QuadratureOperator
docs.text:
Bases: LinearOperator

A scalar linear measurement defined by weighted function evaluations.

Subclasses implement quadrature(point) to return evaluation points of shape (q, d) and weights of shape (q,). Both may depend on the query location and operator parameters, but not on the function being evaluated. Weights may be signed and are not normalized by this class.

The rule must use JAX-compatible operations and keep q fixed under tracing. apply supports JIT, batching, and differentiation through the points and weights. It also preserves trailing function-output axes when operators are nested during covariance compilation.

def apply(self, function: PointFunction, point: Point) -> FunctionalValue:
    self.output_shape(point.shape[-1])
    points, weights = self.quadrature(point)
    values = jax.vmap(function)(points)
    return jnp.tensordot(
        weights, values, axes=(0, 0), precision=jax.lax.Precision.HIGHEST
    )

docs.title: TensorQuadratureOperator
docs.text:
Bases: QuadratureOperator

A scalar quadrature rule that factors over input coordinates.

Implement coordinate_quadrature(point) to return one pair of node and weight vectors per coordinate. Nodes are absolute coordinate values, and full weights are products of coordinate weights. Both may depend on the entire query point and operator parameters, independently of the function. Node counts are static under tracing and may differ between coordinates.

The inherited apply evaluates the Cartesian-product rule. Covariance evaluation with a SeparableKernel contracts coordinate rules directly, preserving the same approximation without constructing the full grid. Overrides of apply or quadrature must represent that same rule.

def quadrature(self, point: Point) -> QuadratureRule:
    rules = self.coordinate_quadrature(point)
    points = jnp.stack(
        jnp.meshgrid(*(nodes for nodes, _ in rules), indexing="ij"), axis=-1
    ).reshape(-1, point.shape[-1])
    weights = jnp.prod(
        jnp.stack(
            jnp.meshgrid(*(weights for _, weights in rules), indexing="ij"),
            axis=-1,
        ),
        axis=-1,
    ).reshape(-1)
    return points, weights

def apply(self, function: PointFunction, point: Point) -> FunctionalValue:
    def second_derivative(axis: int) -> FunctionalValue:
        tangent = jax.nn.one_hot(axis, point.shape[0])

        def first_derivative(variable: Point) -> FunctionalValue:
            return jax.jvp(function, (variable,), (tangent,))[1]

        return jax.jvp(first_derivative, (point,), (tangent,))[1]

    def accumulate(axis: int, total: FunctionalValue) -> FunctionalValue:
        return total + second_derivative(axis)

    # Preserve array-valued intermediate functions from another operator.
    initial = jnp.zeros_like(function(point))
    return jax.lax.fori_loop(0, point.shape[0], accumulate, initial)

BoxAverage(
    radius: BoxRadius | float, *, quadrature_order: int = 8
)

Bases: TensorQuadratureOperator

Average a scalar function over a box centered at each input location.

A scalar radius defines a square or hypercube. A radius vector defines one half-width per input dimension. The integral is approximated by a symmetric tensor-product midpoint rule with quadrature_order ** dimension points.

Construction and evaluation support JIT, batching, and differentiation of finite positive radius values. Quadrature order remains static.

def __init__(self, radius: BoxRadius | float, *, quadrature_order: int = 8) -> None:
    radius = jnp.asarray(radius)
    if radius.ndim > 1 or radius.size == 0:
        raise ValueError("box-average radius must be scalar or one-dimensional")
    if quadrature_order < 1:
        raise ValueError("quadrature order must be positive")
    self.radius = error_if(
        radius,
        jnp.any(~jnp.isfinite(radius) | (radius <= 0)),
        "box-average radius must be finite and strictly positive",
    )
    self.quadrature_order = quadrature_order

def coordinate_quadrature(self, point: Point) -> TensorQuadratureRule:
    input_dimension = point.shape[-1]
    radius = jnp.broadcast_to(self.radius, (input_dimension,))
    normalized_nodes = (
        2.0 * (jnp.arange(self.quadrature_order) + 0.5) / self.quadrature_order
        - 1.0
    )
    weights = jnp.full((self.quadrature_order,), 1.0 / self.quadrature_order)
    return tuple(
        (point[axis] + normalized_nodes * radius[axis], weights)
        for axis in range(input_dimension)
    )

GaussianSmoothing(
    scale: GaussianScale | float,
    *,
    quadrature_order: int = 8,

Bases: TensorQuadratureOperator

Average a scalar function under a centered Gaussian density.

A scalar scale defines an isotropic Gaussian. A scale vector defines one standard deviation per input dimension. The expectation is approximated with tensor-product Gauss--Hermite quadrature using quadrature_order ** dimension points.

Construction and evaluation support JIT, batching, and differentiation of finite positive scale values. Quadrature order remains static.

Source code in src/gpex/operators/quadrature.py 
def __init__(
    self, scale: GaussianScale | float, *, quadrature_order: int = 8
) -> None:
    scale = jnp.asarray(scale)
    if scale.ndim > 1 or scale.size == 0:
        raise ValueError(
            "Gaussian-smoothing scale must be scalar or one-dimensional"
        )
    nodes, weights = np.polynomial.hermite.hermgauss(quadrature_order)
    self.scale = error_if(
        scale,
        jnp.any(~jnp.isfinite(scale) | (scale <= 0)),
        "Gaussian-smoothing scale must be finite and strictly positive",
    )
    self.quadrature_order = quadrature_order
    self._nodes = tuple(float(node * np.sqrt(2.0)) for node in nodes)
    self._weights = tuple(float(weight / np.sqrt(np.pi)) for weight in weights)

def quadrature(self, point: Point) -> QuadratureRule:
    nodes = jnp.asarray(self._nodes)
    weights = jnp.asarray(self._weights)

def quadrature(self, point: Point) -> QuadratureRule:
    nodes = (jnp.arange(self.quadrature_order) + 0.5) / self.quadrature_order
    half_width = self.scale / 2.0
    left_offsets = -half_width + nodes * half_width
    right_offsets = nodes * half_width
    offsets = jnp.concatenate((left_offsets, right_offsets))[:, None]
    signs = jnp.concatenate(
        (jnp.ones(self.quadrature_order), -jnp.ones(self.quadrature_order))
    )
    weights = signs * jnp.sqrt(self.scale) / (2 * self.quadrature_order)
    return point + offsets, weights

docs.title: Parameter values
docs.text:
Only explicit Parameter leaves are fitted. Plain numbers and arrays remain fixed. Parameters store unconstrained optimization coordinates and expose the model value through .value.

Constructor Initial value Constraint Parameter(unconstrained=...) Optimization coordinates Identity transform by default PositiveParameter(value) Positive model value Softplus CholeskyParameter(value) Lower-triangular model matrix Positive diagonal and zero upper triangle

PositiveParameter is used for trainable kernel variance, lengthscales, and scalar observation-noise variance. CholeskyParameter is used for a full input precision factor. A custom transform supplies forward and inverse. Pass transform.inverse(value) to the base constructor's unconstrained argument when starting from a constrained value.

See Fitting hyperparameters for a complete example.

docs.title: Priors
docs.text:
A prior's log_prob receives the constrained model value and returns one scalar joint log density. Scalar prior families sum independent contributions for array-valued parameters. MultivariateLogNormalPrior describes the joint normal distribution of the log-values. A correlated prior on ARD lengthscales still uses an axis-aligned kernel metric.

MAP requires a prior on every trainable parameter. MLE ignores attached priors. The optimization transform adds no Jacobian term to the MAP objective, which is defined on the constrained model values.

For a full precision factor L, IndependentCholeskyPrior uses separate priors for positive diagonal and unconstrained strict-lower entries. ScaledLKJCholeskyPrior describes L = diag(scales) @ C, with positive scales and a correlation Cholesky factor C. These correlations describe the input precision metric. The prior includes the density correction from scales and correlation coordinates to the free entries of L.

Custom priors provide a scalar log_prob(value). Built-in transforms and priors implement the Transform and Prior interfaces below.

def forward(self, unconstrained: ParameterValue) -> ParameterValue:
    rows, columns = jnp.tril_indices(self.dimension)
    # Transform only the diagonal: unrestricted entries remain untouched.
    diagonal = jnp.arange(self.dimension)

    )
    return (
        jnp.zeros((self.dimension, self.dimension)).at[rows, columns].set(entries)
    )

def log_prior(tree: Any, *, require_all: bool = False) -> Scalar:
    """Sum priors explicitly attached to all parameters in a PyTree."""
    parameters = jax.tree_util.tree_leaves(
        tree, is_leaf=lambda item: isinstance(item, Parameter)
    )
    parameters = [item for item in parameters if isinstance(item, Parameter)]
    if not parameters:
        return jnp.zeros(())
    if require_all:
        missing = [
            parameter.name or "<unnamed>"
            for parameter in parameters
            if parameter.prior is None
        ]
        if missing:
            raise ValueError(
                "MAP requires explicit priors for every Parameter; missing: "
                + ", ".join(missing)
            )
    return sum((parameter.log_prior() for parameter in parameters), jnp.zeros(()))

def __init__(
    self,
    log_mean: ArrayLike,
    log_covariance: ArrayLike,
) -> None:
    mean = np.asarray(log_mean)
    covariance = np.asarray(log_covariance)
    # Conversion to Python floats below would discard NumPy imaginary parts.
    if np.iscomplexobj(mean) or np.iscomplexobj(covariance):
        raise ValueError("log mean and covariance must be real")
    if mean.ndim != 1 or mean.size == 0 or not np.all(np.isfinite(mean)):
        raise ValueError("log mean must be a nonempty finite vector")
    if covariance.shape != (mean.size, mean.size):
        raise ValueError("log covariance must have shape (d, d) matching log mean")
    if not np.all(np.isfinite(covariance)) or not np.allclose(
        covariance, covariance.T, rtol=1e-7, atol=1e-12
    ):
        raise ValueError("log covariance must be finite and symmetric")
    covariance = 0.5 * (covariance + covariance.T)
    try:
        factor = np.linalg.cholesky(covariance)
    except np.linalg.LinAlgError as error:
        raise ValueError("log covariance must be positive definite") from error
    object.__setattr__(self, "log_mean", tuple(float(x) for x in mean))
    object.__setattr__(
        self,
        "log_covariance",
        tuple(tuple(float(x) for x in row) for row in covariance),
    )
    object.__setattr__(
        self, "_scale_tril", tuple(tuple(float(x) for x in row) for row in factor)
    )

def log_prob(self, value: ParameterValue) -> Scalar:
    """Return the scalar joint log density, or ``-inf`` outside support.

    Args:
        value: Positive finite vector with shape ``(d,)``.

    Returns:
        Scalar log density with respect to the positive vector. Entries that are
            nonpositive or nonfinite give a density of ``-inf``.
    """
    value = jnp.asarray(value)
    if value.shape != (len(self.log_mean),):
        raise ValueError("prior value must have shape (d,) matching log mean")
    if jnp.issubdtype(value.dtype, jnp.complexfloating):
        raise ValueError("prior value must be real")
    valid = (value > 0) & jnp.isfinite(value)
    log_value = jnp.log(jnp.where(valid, value, 1.0))
    mean = jnp.asarray(self.log_mean)
    factor = jnp.asarray(self._scale_tril)
    standardized = jsp.linalg.solve_triangular(factor, log_value - mean, lower=True)
    log_density = (
        -0.5 * jnp.sum(standardized**2)
        - jnp.sum(jnp.log(jnp.diag(factor)))
        - 0.5 * value.size * jnp.log(2 * jnp.pi)
        - jnp.sum(log_value)
    )
    return jnp.where(jnp.all(valid), log_density, -jnp.inf)
