def log_prob(self, value: ParameterValue) -> Scalar:
    """Return the joint log density, or ``-inf`` outside Cholesky support."""
    value = validate_factor_shape(value)
    valid = is_cholesky_factor(value)
    dimension = value.shape[0]
    matrix = jnp.where(valid, value, jnp.eye(dimension))
    # Scale before squaring to avoid overflow for finite large factors.
    row_max = jnp.max(jnp.abs(matrix), axis=1)
    scales = row_max * jnp.sqrt(jnp.sum((matrix / row_max[:, None]) ** 2, axis=1))
    log_scales = jnp.log(scales)
    log_diagonal = jnp.log(jnp.diag(matrix)) - log_scales

    # Row i (zero-based) has i free correlation coordinates in a unit ball.
    # Integrating its density gives pi**(i/2) * Gamma(a) / Gamma(a+i/2).
    rows = jnp.arange(1.0, dimension)
    alpha = self.concentration + (dimension - 1 - rows) / 2
    log_normalizer = jnp.sum(
        rows / 2 * jnp.log(jnp.pi)
        + jsp.special.gammaln(alpha)
        - jsp.special.gammaln(alpha + rows / 2)
    )
    lkj_density = jnp.sum((2 * alpha - 2) * log_diagonal[1:]) - log_normalizer
    # |d L_i / d (scale_i, C_i)| = scale_i**i / C_ii.
    log_jacobian = jnp.sum(rows * log_scales[1:] - log_diagonal[1:])
    density = self.scale_prior.log_prob(scales) + lkj_density - log_jacobian
    return jnp.where(valid, density, -jnp.inf)

docs.title: JAX and observation capacity
docs.text: A sequential experiment adds observations over time. JAX specializes compiled functions to array shapes, so growing an array can require another compilation at every step. gpex observation blocks can reserve space in advance, keeping their shapes fixed as observations arrive.

docs.title: Observed locations and reserved locations
docs.text:
Suppose an experiment starts with three observations and will collect at most twenty. Reserve twenty locations when constructing the observation block:

import jax.numpy as jnp

from gpex import ObservationBlock

observations = ObservationBlock.from_arrays(
    points=jnp.array([[-1.0], [0.0], [1.0]]),
    y=jnp.array([-0.8, 0.0, 0.8]),
    variance=0.01,
    name="measurements",
    max_size=20,
)

This block has observations.count == 3 active locations and observations.capacity == 20 reserved locations. Only the three observations inform the posterior. Appending two observations increases the count to five and leaves the capacity at twenty. An append beyond capacity raises an error.

max_size counts locations. Each location can contribute several scalar outputs, as specified by the operator. A gradient block in two dimensions with capacity twenty reserves forty scalar outputs. Queries use their supplied locations without reserving additional space.

The default capacity is max(1024, number_of_supplied_locations). For a fixed dataset, pass max_size=points.shape[0] to use compact storage. For an experiment, choose the capacity from its planned number of measurements. Dense conditioning uses quadratic memory and cubic factorization work in the total reserved scalar capacity, including unused space. Each observation block contributes its own reserve.

docs.title: Reusing compiled code
docs.text:
A compiled conditioning function can accept blocks whose active counts change while their reserved shapes stay fixed. Locations, readings, and noise values may also change. Keep the compiled function and pass the current data to it. The sequential observations tutorial shows how to append readings to an existing posterior.

Block names, operator structure, capacities, array shapes, and dtypes determine which compiled program can be reused. Changing those can trigger compilation. Prediction also specializes to query structure and shapes. A different append batch size can compile another update function even when it fits within the same capacity.

When model parameters change, pass the model as an argument to the compiled function. Compiling gp.condition directly captures that particular immutable GP. Constructing and compiling a new closure on every iteration loses the opportunity to reuse the existing compiled function.

docs.title: Updating a dataset and updating a posterior
docs.text:
An observation block stores the measurements. A conditioned posterior stores the result of inference. Their update methods have different purposes:

Operation Result observations.append(locations, readings) A new observation block containing the additional data observations.replace(points, readings) A new block with replacement data and the same capacity gp.condition(dataset) A posterior calculated from the dataset and current model parameters posterior.append(locations, readings, block="measurements") A posterior updated using its existing factorization

All four return new objects. Keep the dataset if you will later fit hyperparameters or replace observations.

Posterior append assumes the kernel, mean, operator parameters, noise, and numerical settings stay fixed. Under those conditions, it gives the same posterior as conditioning on all observations, up to floating-point error. A single scalar append costs quadratic work in reserved scalar capacity. Reusing a compiled condition call still performs the full factorization.

After fitting hyperparameters, replacing readings, or introducing another named block, condition on the complete dataset again. Rebuild any PreparedQuery when its conditioning state or target changes.

docs.title: Blocks for future observations
docs.text:
An experiment can declare a block before any of its readings are available. Use empty arrays with their intended shapes, choose a capacity, and provide a padding_point valid for the kernel and operator:

future = ObservationBlock.from_arrays(
    points=jnp.empty((0, 1)),
    y=jnp.empty((0,)),
    variance=0.01,
    name="future_measurements",
    max_size=10,
    padding_point=jnp.array([0.0]),
)

The block contributes no observations until it receives readings. Its name, operator, and noise variance are already available to the compiled update. See the block reference for constructor arguments and shapes.

docs.title: Gaussian processes with linear functionals
docs.text:
gpex models one unknown scalar-valued function \(f(x)\), where \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is an input location. This is the latent function: the underlying function whose values, derivatives, or averages we may observe and want to predict. A Gaussian process (GP) describes uncertainty about it:

\[ f \sim \mathcal{GP}(m, k). \]

Here \(m(x)\) is the mean of \(f(x)\), and the kernel \(k(x, x')\) is the covariance between \(f(x)\) and \(f(x')\) at two input locations. The GP assumption means that the function values at any finite collection of locations are jointly Gaussian.

docs.title: Linear transformations of a GP
docs.text:
A linear operator \(L\) maps a function \(f\) to another function \(Lf\). For example, the identity gives \((Lf)(x)=f(x)\), a partial derivative gives \((Lf)(x)=\partial f(x)/\partial x_r\), and a local averaging operator gives the average of \(f\) over a region around \(x\).

Linearity refers to the operator's action on functions. For functions \(u,v\) and scalar coefficients \(a,b\), it means

\[ L(au+bv) = aLu+bLv. \]

Neither \(f\) nor \(Lf\) needs to be a linear function of the input \(x\). The operator and its parameters are fixed independently of the realization of \(f\).

A GP remains Gaussian under a linear transformation, provided the transformed quantities are well defined in mean square. In particular, derivatives require sufficient kernel smoothness, and integrals require finite second moments. The transformed process has distribution

\[ Lf \sim \mathcal{GP}(Lm,\, L_x L_{x'}k). \]

The transformed mean is obtained by applying \(L\) to the original mean function. Its covariance kernel is obtained by applying \(L\) to both arguments of the original kernel:

\[ m_L(x) = (Lm)(x), \qquad k_L(x,x') = L_x L_{x'} k(x,x'). \]

The subscripts indicate which argument the operator acts on. Here \(x'\) is a second input location, not a derivative. This is the process analogue of transforming a Gaussian vector \(z\) by a matrix \(A\): its mean becomes \(A\mathbb{E}[z]\) and its covariance becomes \(A\operatorname{cov}(z)A^\top\).

For example, for a sufficiently smooth one-dimensional GP, the derivative is itself a GP:

\[ f' \sim \mathcal{GP}\!\left(m',\, \frac{\partial^2 k(x,x')}{\partial x\,\partial x'}\right). \]

An operator can also produce several components at each location. The gradient \(\nabla f\) is a vector-valued GP derived from the scalar latent function. Its covariance is matrix-valued, with one entry for each pair of gradient components.

docs.title: Different quantities share one latent function
docs.text:
Two linear transformations \(Lf\) and \(Mf\) are jointly Gaussian, with cross-covariance

\[ \operatorname{cov}[(Lf)(x),(Mf)(x')] = L_x M_{x'}k(x,x'). \]

For example, the covariance between a function value and a derivative in one dimension is

\[ \operatorname{cov}[f(x),f'(x')] = \frac{\partial k(x,x')}{\partial x'}. \]

These cross-covariances allow a value observation to inform a derivative prediction and conversely. Values, derivatives, and averages are coupled through the same latent function. gpex constructs their joint Gaussian distribution from the operators and the shared kernel, so mixed measurements can all contribute to one posterior over \(f\).

Fixing a location in \((Lf)(x)\), and selecting one component if needed, produces a scalar linear functional of \(f\). If \(L_i\) and \(L_j\) denote two such functionals, then

\[ \mathbb{E}[L_i f] = L_i m, \qquad \operatorname{cov}[L_i f,L_j f] = L_i L_j' k. \]

In this notation the prime on \(L_j'\) marks action on the second kernel argument. For point evaluations \(L_i f=f(x_i)\) and \(L_j f=f(x_j)\), the covariance reduces to \(k(x_i,x_j)\).

docs.title: What an operator looks like in gpex
docs.text:
GaussianProcess specifies the mean and kernel of the latent function \(f\). A LinearOperator describes the transformation \(L\) through two methods:

  • output_shape(input_dimension) declares the output shape at one location.
  • apply(function, point) computes \((L\,\text{function})(\text{point})\).

For example, the built-in Gradient operator differentiates the supplied callable with JAX:

from collections.abc import Callable

import jax

from gpex.operators import LinearOperator


class Gradient(LinearOperator):
    @property
    def derivative_order(self) -> int:
        return 1

    def output_shape(self, input_dimension: int) -> tuple[int, ...]:
        return (input_dimension,)

    def apply(
        self, function: Callable[[jax.Array], jax.Array], point: jax.Array
    ) -> jax.Array:
        return jax.jacfwd(function)(point)

For a scalar callable and a point of shape (d,), apply returns a gradient of shape (d,). The derivative_order property declares the smoothness required of the latent GP. The identity operator instead returns function(point) and declares scalar output shape ().

During inference, gpex applies these operators to the mean function and to the kernel arguments to construct the transformed means and covariances. Differential operators use automatic differentiation, while built-in integral and averaging operators use explicit quadrature rules.

A FunctionalBlock combines an operator with locations and a name. At \(n\) locations in \(d\) dimensions, Identity() gives a block of shape (n,), while Gradient() gives (n, d). These blocks describe the finite collections of functionals used for observations and queries. See Getting started and Learning a function from derivatives for their use in inference, or Implementing custom operators for a complete extension example.

docs.title: Consequences for modelling
docs.text:
The operator affects what the data identify. Gradients and increments, for example, do not identify a constant offset on their own. Averaging operators attenuate short-scale structure. Derivative observations also require the kernel to possess the corresponding mean-square derivatives.

See Linear operators for the built-in operators and their conventions.

docs.title: Linear operators
docs.text:
An operator describes what a measurement tells us about the unknown function, or which quantity we want to predict. For a spatial temperature field, for example, we might observe the temperature at a point, an average over a sensor's footprint, or the rate of change in a particular direction.

gpex supports all of these as observations and prediction targets. They can be mixed in one model because they are linear transformations of one latent Gaussian process. The operator describes the measured quantity, while observation noise describes uncertainty in the reading.

docs.title: Built-in operators
docs.text:
Write \(f\) for the latent function and \(x\) for a location in \(d\) dimensions. For the averaging formulas, \(B_r(x)\) is the box centered at \(x\) with half-widths \(r\), and \(\varphi_s\) is a centered Gaussian density with independent coordinates and standard deviations \(s\). A scalar radius or scale uses the same width in every coordinate.

The integral formulas describe the continuous quantities. gpex approximates these integrals with numerical quadrature.

The output is the quantity at one location. A vector or matrix output still comes from the same scalar latent function.

docs.title: Values, changes, and curvature
docs.text:
Identity represents an ordinary point measurement. Increment measures the total change between two points separated by a displacement \(h\). It does not divide by the distance between them, and it can be used even when the latent function is not differentiable.

Derivatives describe local rates of change. PartialDerivative selects one coordinate, DirectionalDerivative selects a direction \(v\), and Gradient collects all coordinate derivatives. A unit vector \(v\) gives the rate per unit distance in that direction. Scaling \(v\) scales the directional derivative.

Hessian describes local curvature, including mixed derivatives that relate changes along different coordinates. Laplacian sums the coordinate second derivatives into one scalar, as used in diffusion and Poisson equations. These operators let gpex incorporate slope or curvature measurements and predict them from other observations, such as function values.

Derivative observations and predictions require a sufficiently smooth latent GP. First derivatives need less smoothness than Hessians or Laplacians. See Choosing a kernel for the supported derivative orders.

docs.title: Measurements over a region
docs.text:
BoxAverage models a measurement with a finite footprint, such as a pixel or a sensor that averages over a rectangular area. Every part of the box has equal weight. The radius \(r\) is its half-width, so a one-dimensional box spans from \(x-r\) to \(x+r\).

GaussianSmoothing gives more weight to nearby values, with the weight decreasing smoothly with distance. This can describe a blurred measurement without a sharp boundary. Its scale \(s\) is the Gaussian standard deviation. Both averaging operators preserve constant functions and have the same units as \(f\). Their widths set the spatial scale over which variation is averaged.

CumulativeIntegral1D measures an accumulated quantity from a fixed base \(b\) to the query location \(x\), such as a total amount obtained by integrating a rate. Its value is zero at \(b\), and reversing the integration limits reverses the sign.

HaarWavelet1D measures a contrast between the left and right halves of an interval centered at \(x\). Its scale \(s\) is the full interval width. The coefficient is positive when the left half has the larger average, negative when the right half does, and zero for a constant function. The factor \(1/\sqrt{s}\) gives the analyzing wavelet unit \(L^2\) norm. Both the cumulative integral and Haar wavelet are restricted to one-dimensional inputs.

gpex evaluates these regional measurements using weighted function evaluations, called quadrature. Increasing the quadrature order uses more evaluation points. Accuracy should be checked at the spatial scales relevant to the model. Learning from averages shows why accurately measured averages can leave individual function values uncertain.

docs.title: Factored tensor quadrature
docs.text:
A SeparableKernel expresses a covariance as a product of one-dimensional kernels. A TensorQuadratureOperator describes a quadrature rule through nodes and weights for each coordinate. When these interfaces meet, gpex evaluates one-dimensional quadrature sums and multiplies the results.

For two rules with q nodes along each of d coordinates, this needs d * q² coordinate-kernel evaluations rather than q^(2d) full-kernel evaluations. RBFKernel provides the separable representation for scalar and ARD lengthscales. BoxAverage and GaussianSmoothing provide tensor rules. Custom implementations of these interfaces receive the same optimization, as do separable components of kernel sums.

This rearranges the same quadrature approximation. It does not remove its integration error. Generic kernels and kernel products use the general calculation. Mean and feature evaluation still expand the full tensor grid. The optimization also applies when a tensor rule occurs on only one side of a covariance. See the kernel interfaces and quadrature interfaces.

docs.title: Combining operators
docs.text:
A single reading may combine several effects. LinearCombination forms one operator from component operators \(L_j\) and fixed coefficients \(c_j\). For example, a sensor that responds to both the function value and a slope can be described by

\[ (Lf)(x) = a f(x)+b\frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x_j}. \]

The component operators must have matching outputs: scalars can be added to scalars, or vectors of the same size to each other. To model separate readings of different quantities, use separate observation blocks. Those readings can have different operators, locations, and noise levels while informing one posterior.

docs.title: What the measurements can reveal
docs.text:
Derivative measurements do not tell us the function's vertical offset. We can shift a function up or down without changing any of its derivatives. Increments and Haar coefficients have the same limitation. A function value or an average measurement helps pin down that offset.

An average can hide small fluctuations. A flat function and one that rises and falls around the same value can have the same average over a region. Measuring that average does not tell us which function we have. The kernel describes how much fluctuation the GP expects, while measurements at individual points or over smaller regions can help reveal it.

See Learning a function from derivatives for the effect of adding a single value to derivative measurements, and Learning from averages for the variation left uncertain by window measurements. Other linear measurements can be expressed with custom operators. Constructor arguments and method details are listed in the operator API reference.

docs.title: Observations, designs, and queries
docs.text:
gpex separates the quantity being measured, the uncertainty of the measurement, and the reading obtained. The same function value can be described before an experiment is performed and then paired with its reading afterwards.

Object Contains Role FunctionalBlock locations, operator, name quantities to measure or predict ObservationDesignBlock functional block and measurement-error variance planned measurements ObservationBlock design and readings y realized measurements

The following sections build these objects in order, using the function-value measurements from Getting started.

docs.title: Describe the quantity to measure
docs.text:
Suppose we want to measure an unknown function \(f\) at three locations in one dimension. A FunctionalBlock describes those quantities through their locations and operator. Identity() means evaluating \(f\) itself at each location. The name "observed_values" identifies this group of quantities.

import jax.numpy as jnp

from gpex import FunctionalBlock, operators

points = jnp.array([[-1.0], [0.0], [1.0]])
functional = FunctionalBlock(
    locations=points,
    operator=operators.Identity(),
    name="observed_values",
)

Each row of points specifies one location. This block describes the three latent values \(f(-1)\), \(f(0)\), and \(f(1)\). It does not yet specify measurement error or contain readings.

docs.title: Designs specify measurements before readings
docs.text:
A reading may differ from the latent function value because of measurement error. An ObservationDesignBlock adds the variance of that error to the functional block. For this example, choose a variance of 0.01 for every reading. At each location \(x_i\), the reading \(y_i\) is modelled as

\[ y_i = f(x_i) + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.01). \]

The errors are independent of one another and of the latent function.

ObservationDesign collects one or more design blocks:

from gpex import ObservationDesign, ObservationDesignBlock

design_block = ObservationDesignBlock(functional=functional, variance=0.01)
design = ObservationDesign(blocks=[design_block])

Here the design contains just the planned value measurements at our three locations. Each block shares one error variance across its measurements. Separate blocks can represent measurements with different variances.

The design is complete before any readings are available: it states what will be measured, where, and with what measurement uncertainty.

docs.title: Datasets contain realized measurements
docs.text:
Once the measurements have been taken, an ObservationBlock attaches the readings to their design. A FunctionalDataset collects these observation blocks for conditioning a GP. Suppose we obtained -0.8, 0.0, and 0.8 at the three locations, in that order:

from gpex import FunctionalDataset, ObservationBlock

readings = jnp.array([-0.8, 0.0, 0.8])
observation = ObservationBlock(design=design_block, y=readings)
dataset = FunctionalDataset(blocks=[observation])

Each entry in readings corresponds to one row of points. These are noisy function-value observations, with the error variance already specified by design_block.

This dataset contains one block. Larger datasets can combine several blocks, each with its own locations, operator, and variance. Block names must be unique within the collection, and all blocks describe measurements of the same latent function on the same input domain.

See Conditioning and prediction for constructing a posterior from the dataset, and Streaming inference for incorporating later readings.

docs.title: Queries describe latent quantities
docs.text:
After observing function values, we may want to predict how quickly the function changes between the measurement locations. This is a different quantity of the same latent function: its derivative. In one dimension, Gradient() returns that derivative at each location.

A FunctionalQuery collects the functional blocks we want to predict. Here we ask for derivatives at -0.5 and 0.5:

from gpex import FunctionalQuery

target_points = jnp.array([[-0.5], [0.5]])
target_gradient = FunctionalBlock(
    locations=target_points,
    operator=operators.Gradient(),
    name="target_gradient",
)
query = FunctionalQuery(blocks=[target_gradient])

The query contains no readings or measurement-error variance. It describes the latent derivatives whose distribution we want to predict. The name "target_gradient" identifies their means, variances, or samples in a prediction result. The observed function values inform these derivatives through their shared GP, as explained in Gaussian processes with linear functionals.

Designs and queries also work together when planning a future experiment: the design specifies the proposed measurements, and the query specifies the quantities whose uncertainty we want to reduce. For example, we could compare possible value measurements by how much they would reduce uncertainty about these target derivatives. With the GP parameters fixed, the conditional covariance can be calculated before the future readings are known. See Experimental design for this workflow.

docs.title: Access the measurement description
docs.text:
The observation retains the design that gives its readings meaning. Its functional block describes the underlying latent values, while its design also specifies the measurement-error variance:

observation.functional             # descriptions of f(-1), f(0), and f(1)
observation.functional.operator    # Identity()
observation.functional.name        # "observed_values"
observation.design                 # the design_block used above
observation.design.variance        # 0.01
observation.y                      # stored readings

A design also exposes a query through design.query. For the design above, this describes the underlying function values at the measurement locations. A prediction for this query excludes measurement error. To obtain the covariance of future noisy readings at those locations, add the measurement-error variance to the covariance diagonal.

docs.title: A convenience constructor for observed data
docs.text:
When locations and readings are already available, ObservationBlock.from_arrays constructs the functional and design blocks for you. Its default operator is Identity(), so the following is a shorter way to create the same value observations and dataset as above:

observation = ObservationBlock.from_arrays(
    points=points,
    y=readings,
    variance=0.01,
    name="observed_values",
)
dataset = FunctionalDataset(blocks=[observation])

For array shapes and numerical setup, see Getting started. Storage capacity and compiled updates are covered in Reuse compiled conditioning.

docs.text:

class TangentLift(LinearOperator):
    """Multiply a function value by the unit-circle tangent at an angle."""

    def output_shape(self, input_dimension: int) -> tuple[int, ...]:
        if input_dimension != 1:
            raise ValueError("TangentLift expects one angle")
        return (2,)

    def apply(
        self,
        function: Callable[[jax.Array], jax.Array],
        point: Float[Array, "1"],
    ) -> Float[Array, "*existing 2"]:
        theta = point[0]
        tangent = jnp.stack((-jnp.sin(theta), jnp.cos(theta)))
        return function(point)[..., None] * tangent


velocity_operator = TangentLift()
class TangentLift(LinearOperator): """Multiply a function value by the unit-circle tangent at an angle.""" def output_shape(self, input_dimension: int) -> tuple[int, ...]: if input_dimension != 1: raise ValueError("TangentLift expects one angle") return (2,) def apply( self, function: Callable[[jax.Array], jax.Array], point: Float[Array, "1"], ) -> Float[Array, "*existing 2"]: theta = point[0] tangent = jnp.stack((-jnp.sin(theta), jnp.cos(theta))) return function(point)[..., None] * tangent velocity_operator = TangentLift()

The [..., None] adds the two-component axis after any existing output axes. For a scalar function the result has shape (2,). If the supplied function already returns an array of shape (m,), the result has shape (m, 2). gpex needs this preservation of existing axes when it applies operators to both arguments of a kernel to construct covariances.

docs.title: Implementing a custom operator¶
docs.text:
Suppose sensors on a circular arc measure a two-component velocity: one horizontal component and one vertical component. We know the underlying velocity is tangent to the arc, but its strength and direction vary with angle.

We can describe this with one scalar function $f(\theta)$, the signed tangential velocity. On the unit circle, the known unit tangent and the velocity vector are

$$ \mathbf t(\theta) = (-\sin\theta,\cos\theta), \qquad \mathbf v(\theta) = f(\theta)\,\mathbf t(\theta). $$

Positive $f(\theta)$ points toward increasing angle, and negative values reverse the direction. Our GP models $f$, while the sensors observe noisy versions of both components of $\mathbf v$. We'll infer $f$ and predict vectors on the same open arc, with angles between $-1.2$ and $1.2$ radians.

docs.title: Turn a scalar value into a tangent vector¶
docs.text:
Multiplication by the known tangent is linear in the function: scaling or adding functions scales or adds their velocity vectors in the same way. The tangent depends only on the angle, not on the unknown function.

To express this as a custom LinearOperator, implement two methods. output_shape declares the two components produced at each angle. apply evaluates the supplied function at that angle and multiplies its value by the tangent.

docs.title: Generate vector readings¶
docs.text:
We'll use a known scalar function to generate five synthetic readings, with uneven sensor locations and a gap near the middle of the arc. Applying our operator gives the true vectors. We then add independent Gaussian measurement errors with variance 0.02 to each component.

The GP input is the one-entry array [theta]. The Cartesian position (cos(theta), sin(theta)) is used to place vectors in the plot.

docs.title: Recover the scalar function and predict vectors¶
docs.text: The identity operator asks for the underlying signed tangential velocity $f(\theta)$. We'll use predict_marginals to obtain its posterior mean and variance for a pointwise 95% interval.

docs.title: Experimental design¶
docs.text: Where should we observe a function if we want to learn its gradient at a particular point? We'll choose a batch of four function-value observations, optimizing their locations together to reduce uncertainty in that gradient.

docs.title: Describe the existing observations¶
docs.text:
Our function has two input coordinates. We already have eight function-value observations around the edge of a square, each with error variance 0.02. We use an RBF kernel with lengthscale 0.9.

With the kernel parameters and error variances fixed, posterior uncertainty depends on where and how we observe the function, but not on the readings. An ObservationDesign describes just what we need for this calculation: locations, operators, and error variances.

docs.title: Choose the target¶
docs.text:
We want the gradient at (0.25, -0.15): the function's rate of change in each of the two coordinate directions. Gradient() gives us both components.

PreparedQuery caches the calculations for this fixed target and the existing observations. We can reuse it while trying different locations for the new observations.

docs.title: Score the whole batch¶
docs.text:
Our score is the sum of the two gradient variances after adding the four proposed observations. Smaller values mean less uncertainty about the gradient.

We put all four locations in one ObservationDesignBlock and pass it to predict_variance_after. This evaluates their combined information, accounting for overlap between what they tell us. Scoring each observation separately could favor several locations that provide much the same information.

The new observations have error variance 0.02. We restrict their locations to (-2.5, 2.5) in each coordinate by writing them as 2.5 * tanh(parameters).

docs.title: Optimize all four locations¶
docs.text:
jax.value_and_grad evaluates the score and differentiates it with respect to the location parameters. These derivatives tell the optimizer how to move the proposed observations. They are distinct from the gradient of the function that we want to learn.

The helper below takes 180 Adam steps and records the score and locations along the way. jax.lax.scan runs the steps in a loop compiled by jax.jit.

docs.title: First posterior¶
docs.text:
We have three noisy measurements of an unknown one-dimensional function. What can we infer about its values between the measurements, where we have no data? We'll use a Gaussian process to estimate the function on [-2, 2] and show how much uncertainty remains.

Start by enabling 64-bit precision before importing gpex or creating arrays.

docs.title: Record the measurements¶
docs.text: Two measurements are close together on the left, with a third on the right. Each row of x_observed holds one location. This gives it shape (3, 1), with one coordinate per location. y_observed contains the three measured function values in the same order.

docs.title: Choose a prior and condition on the data¶
docs.text:
The GP prior describes the function before seeing these measurements. We'll use an RBF kernel, which models smooth functions. Its lengthscale=0.5 controls how quickly correlation weakens with distance, so nearby function values are more closely related than distant ones. Its variance=1.0 gives a prior standard deviation of one for the function value at each location. The default mean is zero.

Conditioning combines this prior with the measurements and their error variance. The returned posterior describes what we know about the function after observing the data.

docs.title: Ask for function values¶
docs.text:
To see the posterior across the interval, choose a grid of locations and put it in a FunctionalQuery. A FunctionalBlock combines those locations with an operator describing what to evaluate. Here operators.Identity() asks for the function value itself. The name "function" lets us retrieve those results.

predict_marginals computes a mean and variance at each requested location. The mean is our estimate of the function value, and the variance measures our remaining uncertainty about it.

docs.title: Read the posterior¶
docs.text: Plot the mean together with a pointwise 95% posterior interval: the mean plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations at each location. The orange error bars show the same multiple of the assumed measurement-error standard deviation.

docs.title: Learning a function from derivatives¶
docs.text:
Suppose we can measure a function's slope and curvature, but not its value.

We'll combine the two kinds of derivative readings, predict function values and changes between locations, then add a single value measurement. That one reading will reduce uncertainty across the whole interval.

docs.title: Observe slopes and curvature¶
docs.text:
Use a known function to generate a small dataset. We take six noisy slope readings and three noisy curvature readings at different locations. The errors are independent Gaussians with standard deviations 0.08 and 0.15.

PartialDerivative(axis=0) measures $f'(x)$. In one dimension, Laplacian() measures $f''(x)$. An operator's apply method lets us generate the corresponding synthetic reading from our known function.

docs.title: Infer the function from the derivative readings¶
docs.text: Put each sensor type in its own observation block, with its operator and measurement-error variance. Each fixed block reserves just enough space for its readings.

docs.title: Add one value to locate the function's level¶
docs.text: A single value measurement anchors the function. Here we measure it at -0.2, with measurement-error standard deviation 0.05, and combine all three blocks.

docs.title: Fitting hyperparameters¶
docs.text:
The lengthscale and measurement variance affect how a GP explains our data. A short lengthscale allows rapid changes in the function. A large measurement variance allows more of the variation in the observations to be attributed to measurement error. How can we choose these settings from data, and when does prior knowledge change the answer?

We'll fit a GP to fifteen noisy measurements of a sine function. We know the underlying function in this synthetic example, so we can compare our predictions with it. The fitting procedure sees only the measurements.

docs.title: Choose what to fit¶
docs.text:
We'll fit the RBF lengthscale and the measurement-error variance shared by all fifteen observations. The kernel variance stays at 1.0, giving function values a prior scale of order one.

Wrapping a value in PositiveParameter makes it trainable and keeps it positive. Ordinary numbers and arrays stay fixed. The initial values below are starting points for optimization, not constraints on the fitted values.

For the MAP fit, suppose previous experiments suggest a lengthscale around 0.5, and instrument calibration suggests a measurement variance around 0.02. We'll express this knowledge using log-normal priors. Each prior's log_mean is the logarithm of its median, and log_standard_deviation controls its spread. These choices leave room for the data to change our estimates:

Quantity Prior median Approximate central 95% prior range Lengthscale, in location units 0.5 0.25–1.0 Measurement variance, in squared function-value units 0.02 0.0075–0.053

MAP requires a prior for every explicit Parameter. We'll attach them now, but the likelihood-only fit will ignore them.

docs.title: Look at the starting prediction¶
docs.text: Before fitting, let's see what the initial lengthscale 0.25 and measurement variance 0.08 imply. As in First posterior, an identity query asks for function values, and predict_marginals supplies the means and variances for a pointwise 95% interval.

docs.title: Fit by MLE and MAP¶
docs.text:
The short initial lengthscale lets the mean follow local fluctuations, while the interval leaves considerable uncertainty between the observations and outside their range. We'll now let the data inform these settings.

Maximum marginal likelihood (MLE) chooses hyperparameters that make the observed values most probable after averaging over the unknown GP function. Maximum a posteriori estimation (MAP) also uses the parameter priors we specified above. It favors settings that explain the data and have high prior density.

fit_lbfgs minimizes an objective, so we supply the negative log marginal likelihood for MLE and the negative log posterior for MAP. Both fits use the same starting model.

docs.title: Compare the fitted predictions¶
docs.text:
Both fits increase the lengthscale and reduce the measurement variance. For this sample, MLE estimates a measurement variance of about 0.0053. MAP puts it closer to our calibration prior, at about 0.0099, and chooses a somewhat shorter lengthscale than MLE.

Let's condition each fitted GP on its fitted dataset and compare the function predictions on the same axes as before.

docs.title: Learning from averages¶
docs.text:
Suppose a sensor reports the average of a function over a window. A nearly flat function and one that rises and falls can give the same reading. How much can we learn about what happens inside the window?

We'll use three window averages to predict the function, then compare our uncertainty about individual values with our uncertainty about the averages. Then we will use the same observations to predict an accumulated integral.

docs.title: Measure three window averages¶
docs.text:
BoxAverage(radius=0.55) measures the mean over an interval of width 1.1. The locations below are the window centers. For example, the first window covers [-1.65, -0.55]. quadrature_order=24 uses 24 evaluation points to approximate each average.

Use a known function to generate synthetic averages, then add independent Gaussian measurement errors with standard deviation 0.04.

docs.title: Predict the function and its averages¶
docs.text: Put average in the observation block to tell gpex what the sensor measures. The prior's lengthscale of 0.35 allows variation within each window.

docs.title: Predict an accumulated integral¶
docs.text:
Suppose we also want the total accumulated from the left edge of the first window to each location:

$$ I(x) = \int_{-1.65}^{x} f(t)\,\mathrm{d}t. $$

Use CumulativeIntegral1D(base=-1.65) in a new query. The observations remain the same three window averages.

docs.title: Sampling from a GP posterior¶
docs.text:
Sampling lets us explore functions compatible with our measurements. We'll start by sampling function values at a fixed set of locations, then draw a function that we can evaluate at new locations and differentiate.

We use the three observations from First posterior, with measurement-error variance 0.02.

docs.title: Sample values at fixed locations¶
docs.text:
The posterior function values at any fixed set of locations are jointly Gaussian. We can therefore sample them together from a multivariate Gaussian distribution, preserving their correlations.

Let's choose nine locations and draw five samples with posterior.sample. The identity operator asks for function values at those locations.

docs.title: Sample a function¶
docs.text:
A GP is also a distribution over functions. We can draw a function and then evaluate it wherever we need, including locations chosen after the draw.

FeaturePosteriorPath gives us an approximate function draw. Larger feature_count values improve the approximation on average, but make the function slower to evaluate.

docs.title: Differentiate the sampled function¶
docs.text: We can apply operators to the sampled function. Here the RBF kernel gives smooth functions, so we can use jax.grad to differentiate it. Our input has one coordinate, so each gradient has one component: the derivative with respect to location.

for ax in axes[1:]:
    ax.scatter(
        x_first[:, 0], y_first, color="#6D597A", s=35, zorder=4,
        label="First added measurement",
    )
axes[2].scatter(
    x_second[:, 0], y_second, color="#2A7F7F", marker="s", s=35,
    zorder=4, label="Second added measurement",
)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Function value")
handles, labels = axes[2].get_legend_handles_labels()
fig.legend(handles, labels, loc="outside lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False)
plt.show()
fig, axes = plt.subplots( 1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.8), sharex=True, sharey=True, layout="constrained" ) for ax, prediction, title in zip( axes, predictions, ("Initial posterior", "After one append", "After two appends") ): plot_posterior(ax, prediction) ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Location", xlim=(-2, 2)) for ax in axes[1:]: ax.scatter( x_first[:, 0], y_first, color="#6D597A", s=35, zorder=4, label="First added measurement", ) axes[2].scatter( x_second[:, 0], y_second, color="#2A7F7F", marker="s", s=35, zorder=4, label="Second added measurement", ) axes[0].set_ylabel("Function value") handles, labels = axes[2].get_legend_handles_labels() fig.legend(handles, labels, loc="outside lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False) plt.show()

All five reserved locations are now filled. Appending beyond max_size raises an error, so reserve the planned total before conditioning. See JAX and observation capacity for compiling updates, changing capacity, or refitting the model.

docs.title: Sequential observations¶
docs.text: Use posterior.append to add measurements to an existing posterior while reusing the work from conditioning. The GP parameters and measurement-error variance stay fixed between updates.

docs.title: Reserve space for more observations¶
docs.text: Start with the three measurements from First posterior. Set max_size=5 to reserve space for two more observations.

docs.title: Append observations¶
docs.text:
The block argument selects the observation block to extend. New observations use that block's operator and measurement-error variance.

append returns a new posterior. The original posterior and dataset remain unchanged.
